about.tagline: A hardware profiler for Linux. What CPU-Z, GPU-Z and HWMonitor do on Windows, in one native program: what machine you have and what it is doing right now.
about.thanks.why: For the reports they send from their machines: with them Silux is tested on machines that are not ours.

app.frozen: Frozen · press space to carry on

Saved to {ruta}

app.report.title: Save machine report
bat.health.hint: How much of the factory capacity is left. Below 80 % it shows in runtime; that is normal after some 500 cycles.
bat.left.hint: At the current draw. Idle lasts far longer than compiling, and both figures are true.
bat.limit.hint: Your laptop can avoid charging all the way. Stopping at 60 or 80 % noticeably extends cell life if the machine stays plugged in.
bat.nodata: The firmware declares a battery but gives no capacity, charge or voltage.
bat.nodata.impossible: The firmware declares a battery, but gives neither its capacity nor its charge, and the voltage it reports, {tension}, is impossible for one of {nominal} nominal.
bat.nodata.title: Battery without data
bat.power.fromenergy: This machine doesn't give the battery's power: it comes from how much its energy fell or rose between two of the firmware's updates, which come every few seconds.
bench.button.clearold: Delete the ones on another scale
bench.card.title: Benchmark
bench.compare.title: Previous runs on this machine   ·   {signo}{pct}% against the one from {fecha}
bench.cond.endfreq.tip: The average over the last stretch. If it is well below the peak, the processor did not hold its top clock through the run.
bench.cond.load.tip: What was keeping the machine busy right before starting. With background load the result cannot be compared.
bench.cond.maxload.tip: The most another program took while measuring. A fifteen-second run per workload takes two and a half minutes: something waking up halfway through does not show in the figure above, which is taken before starting.
bench.dialog.clear.body:
{n} {plural} from this machine will be deleted.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.clearold.body:
{n} runs measured on a scale older than v{version} will be deleted. The ones on the current scale stay.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.clearold.body.one:
{n} run measured on a scale older than v{version} will be deleted. The ones on the current scale stay.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.delete.body:
«{nombre}» will be deleted.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.duration.body:
How many minutes each of the ten measurements lasts.

The whole run takes ten times this.
bench.dialog.name: Name of the run
bench.dialog.name.body: So you remember what changed between one and the next:
bench.dialog.name.tip: Give it a name: «new thermal paste», «summer»…
bench.drift.cooler: This run peaked {grados} below the median of the {n} previous {pruebas} with the same score. If you have just cleaned it or repasted it, this is where it shows.
bench.drift.hotter: This run peaked {grados} above the median of the {n} previous {pruebas} with the same score. That is usually dust or dried-out thermal paste — or simply a warmer room, which no sensor in the machine measures.
bench.duration.tip:
How long each of the ten measurements lasts: five loads, on one thread and on all of them. The whole run takes ten times this.

Longer ones do not give a higher score: they give the one that holds up once the machine is already warm.
bench.explain.scaling:
Scaling
How much performance multiplies when using every thread. It never reaches the thread count: the ones sharing a core split the same execution units.
bench.history.note: Only from this machine and only on disk: nothing is sent anywhere. Comparing against numbers off the internet hardly ever helps, because they were measured with another governor and another temperature; comparing against yourself does tell you whether something changed.
bench.history.oldscale: {n} of these runs were measured before the benchmark was fixed and with a different scale, so they have no score: their figure would not mean the same as today's. Everything else they recorded is still there.
bench.history.scale.tip: It was measured with another scoring scale; the current one is v{nueva}. Its figure would not mean the same as the current ones, so it is not shown next to them.
bench.intro: Measures the processor with five different loads, first on one thread and then on all of them. The interesting part is not just the number: each load scales differently, and that shows what makes use of the threads and what sits waiting on memory. While it runs, the machine goes flat out.
bench.quick.tip: Eight seconds instead of twenty. Enough to get an idea, but with less room for the turbo to settle.
bench.results.unscored: * Not part of the score: a system library computes it, so its figure changes with the distribution rather than with the processor. It is measured anyway, because it is the one that tells you what is underneath.
bench.score.above: {pct} % above what is usual for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.alone: There is nothing to compare this figure with yet. It is useful to see how this machine changes against itself (between governors, before and after cleaning the heatsink); putting it next to another machine's needs someone else to have measured the same part.
bench.score.below: {pct} % below what is usual for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.normal: It performs as expected for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.onlyown: This figure compares against your own runs of the same length, but not against other machines: that needs the {s} s measurement, which is the only one taken the same way everywhere.
board.na.chipset.codename: Its PCI identification gives the chipset's codename, not a commercial model.
board.na.secureboot.legacy: There is no Secure Boot with legacy BIOS: it belongs to UEFI.
board.nosystem: This is a retail board: the firmware does not describe a branded computer.
board.pci.slots.locked: The name of each slot (“PCIEX16”, “M2A_CPU”) is in the firmware table and appears once permissions are granted.
board.pci.slots.unknown: This board's firmware does not say which slot each device is in.
board.tip.bios: The «System BIOS Release» field of the SMBIOS table. Not the version the maker publishes on its site, but the one the firmware declares about itself.
board.tip.chipset: The full name pci.ids uses for the LPC/eSPI bridge on bus 0, which is what acts as the chipset.
board.tip.memctl: On modern processors it is built into the CPU itself, not the chipset.
board.unfilled: This board's firmware does not give {campos}.
board.virtual: This is a virtual machine: it has no motherboard, and what shows is what the hypervisor declares.
cache.l3.uneven: The L3 is not the same across the processor: {reparto}.
cache.l3.vcache: That is the V-Cache stacked on just one of the two chiplets: a thread that lands on the big one gets more out of memory.
caches.latency.note: Latency is the one measured in Memory (“Bandwidth and latency”): how long an access the processor cannot predict takes. It holds for this session; measure again from there.
caches.line.note: The smallest unit that travels between memory and cache. Reading a single byte pulls in the whole line, which is why walking contiguous data is far faster than jumping around memory.
caches.map.note: Each block is one physical cache instance; its width is the logical CPUs that share it.
caches.subtitle: {n} distinct caches over {nucleos} and {hilos}
caches.virtual: The hypervisor declares them: they need not be the real processor's.
caches.ways.note: An N-way cache stores each address in one of N possible places. More ways reduce clashes between data competing for the same set, at the cost of a more expensive lookup.
cli.description: Silux in the terminal: the computer's hardware and its sensors, without a window.
cli.epilog.report:
The report leaves out the computer name, addresses and serial numbers,
unless you pass --with-identifiers. Bugs go to https://github.com/rcv11x/silux/issues
cli.epilog.title: Examples:
cli.example.json: everything as JSON, for other programs
cli.example.report: the report to attach to a bug
cli.opt.dbinfo: where the processor database comes from
cli.opt.ids: keep in the report what identifies the computer: name, addresses and serial numbers
cli.opt.json: everything as JSON, for other programs
cli.opt.report: write the Markdown report to attach to a bug; without a file, to the screen
cli.opt.short: with --report, the old short report, without mounting the pages
cli.opt.watch: repeat every SECONDS (every second by default)
cli.opt.withoutperms: with --report, do not ask for the password: only what can be read without permissions
cli.report.asking: Asking for permissions to also read what only the administrator sees (--without-permissions skips this)…
cli.report.empty: the report needs a file name, or «-» to print it
cli.report.noqt: Qt cannot start here: writing the short report.
cli.report.unknownsection: There is no section called {names}. These are the ones: {known}.
clock.turbo.capped: The kernel caps it at {actual} of the {max} the silicon can do
clock.turbo.off: Turbo is off: the silicon would reach {max}
core.name: core {n}
core.spread: the weakest one (core {n}) tops out at {pct}% of the best
core.spread.type: the weakest one (core {n}) tops out at {pct}% of the best of its kind
cpu.best.short: {nucleos}{hilos}: the best cores of this processor.
cpu.best.tip: They are the ones that came out best from the wafer according to the firmware, and where the scheduler sends single-thread work. {reparto}.
cpu.clocks.nodriver.cpuinfo: Without a frequency driver there is no governor, energy preference, or kernel minimum and maximum. The frequency is the one the kernel records for each core.
cpu.clocks.nodriver.msr: Without a frequency driver there is no governor, energy preference, or kernel minimum and maximum. The frequency is that of the P-state the processor is in.
cpu.clocks.noepp: {driver} offers no energy preference: intel_pstate in active mode with HWP and amd-pstate in active mode do.
cpu.clocks.noturbo: This processor has no turbo: its highest frequency is the base.
cpu.idle.deepest: {nombre} is this processor's deepest idle state: {tiempo}.
cpu.idle.deepest.acpi: {nombre} is the deepest of the idle states the board declares in its ACPI table, which are the ones Linux uses here: its number is ACPI's, not the processor's. {tiempo}.
cpu.idle.share.range: between {bajo} % and {alto} % of the time, depending on the thread
cpu.idle.title: Over the last interval, averaged across all threads
cpu.limit.amd: AMD's power limits (PPT, TDC and EDC) are not published by the kernel.
cpu.limit.lowest: the lower of the two it declares (the other: {otro})
cpu.limit.lowest.tip: The processor keeps each limit in two places, its registers and the memory controller's, and enforces the lower one. Laptop makers often lower only one of them.
cpu.limit.window.tip: Each limit applies to the average power over its window. The processor can go above PL1, up to PL2, as long as the average over the PL1 window stays below it: that is how long a sustained boost lasts.
cpu.power.headline: {pct} % of {w} W
cpu.subtitle: {nucleos} · {hilos} · {sockets}
cpu.throttle.tip: How many times a core, or the whole processor, reached its temperature limit and lowered its clock since the machine was switched on, and how long that lasted in total. The kernel counts them.
cpu.tip.base.tdp: The base above is the processor's specification, at its nominal TDP. The machine's maker can configure another TDP, which changes the frequency it guarantees: this one.
cpu.tip.voltage: What the processor asks for in its current state. With turbo on, the chip's own microcontroller takes over and the real value goes above this; what actually arrives is measured by the board regulator, when its chip labels the channels.
cpu.virtual.foot: This is a virtual processor: what it declares is up to the hypervisor, so it is not looked up in the processor table, which is where the codename, the process and the package come from.
csv.save.title: Save the sensor log
csv.title: Sensor log
deps.graphics: System graphics libraries are missing ({cuales}): what they would report does not show in «Graphics libraries».
deps.kmod: modinfo and modprobe (kmod) are missing: which kernel modules exist is not known, and none can be loaded from Silux.
deps.nvml: NVML, the NVIDIA driver's library, is missing: without it the card's usage, temperature, power, clocks and memory do not show.
deps.pciids: pci.ids is missing: PCI devices show their number and not their name.
deps.pkexec: pkexec is missing: there is no way to ask for permissions, and what needs them does not show (memory modules, voltage, disk health).
deps.pkexec.nosystemd: Without systemd, polkit also needs elogind and a polkit agent in the session to ask for the password; then log in again.
deps.pkexec.nosystemd.debian: Without systemd, polkit also needs libpam-elogind, which brings elogind, and a polkit agent in the session to ask for the password, such as lxpolkit; then log in again.
deps.pnpids: pnp.ids is missing: each monitor's maker shows its three-letter code and not its name.
deps.polkitagent: pkexec is there, but no polkit agent runs in the session to ask for the password, so permissions can't be given.
deps.polkitagent.hint: Install {paquete} and have it start with your session (in your desktop's or window manager's autostart); then ask for the permissions again.
deps.python3: The system's Python is missing: from the AppImage the permissions helper runs with it, and without it they cannot be given.
deps.systemctl: systemctl is missing: boot times do not show.
deps.usbids: usb.ids is missing: a USB network card shows no model when its own doesn't say it.
deps.xdgopen: xdg-open is missing: the links and folders Silux opens do not open.
dev.bt.none.long: This machine has no Bluetooth adapter.
dev.bt.pie: Only the adapter. Paired devices are not shown: they belong to others.
dev.subtitle: {sonido} · {camaras} · {bluetooth}
dev.usb.pie: Each thing hangs off the hub it is plugged into. Serial numbers are not read.
dev.usb.slow: This device is USB {version} and is negotiating at {velocidad}: it is usually the cable or the port.
disk.trim.unseen: no sign of it being issued
disk.warn.backup: the power-loss backup memory has failed
disk.warn.life: It has {pct}% of its life left, by its own wear counter.
disk.warn.media.many: {n} pieces of data that could not be read since it left the factory.
disk.warn.media.one: {n} piece of data that could not be read since it left the factory.
disk.warn.pmr: its persistent memory region is unreliable
disk.warn.readonly: it has switched to read-only mode
disk.warn.reliability: the drive has downgraded its own reliability
disk.warn.spare: the spare area has dropped below the maker's threshold
disk.warn.temp: the temperature is outside the range it accepts
disk.warn.unknown: The drive is flagging a problem (code {codigo}).
gpu.apis.notasked: Asked when the card asleep wakes up
gpu.apis.notseen: Neither Vulkan nor OpenGL use it on this computer
gpu.apis.rejected: the driver is installed and does not accept this card
gpu.asleep: Asleep: it is not queried, so that it stays asleep.
gpu.codec.name: Codec
gpu.codec.no: Not accelerated: the processor does it
gpu.displays.preferred.only: The resolution of {salidas} is the monitor's preferred one: the one it runs at couldn't be asked.
gpu.displays.unpublished: The driver does not publish its outputs
gpu.engine.name: Engine
gpu.engines.rc6off: RC6 disabled: the GPU never sleeps and draws power even when idle
gpu.expert.off.how: With OverDrive off the driver lets no clock or voltage be changed. It's turned on with bit 14 (0x4000) of the kernel parameter amdgpu.ppfeaturemask, as LACT explains.
gpu.expert.on: on: the driver lets clocks and voltages be changed
gpu.na.amd.caches: amdgpu gives the caches' size from RDNA 3 (gfx11) on: for this generation it doesn't.
gpu.na.amd.silent: Its driver doesn't publish, on this card, {campos}.
gpu.na.apu: On an APU, the power the driver reports is that of the whole processor and its second temperature is the SoC's: neither belongs to the graphics.
gpu.na.arc.link: An Arc's PCIe link is not shown: its internal switch reports 2.5 GT/s × 1 on the inside, and the side that talks to the motherboard cannot be told apart reliably.
gpu.na.integrated: Voltage regulators and the fan belong to a separate card: this one is powered and cooled along with the rest of the machine.
gpu.na.intel.card: i915 does not count render output units or shader engines: Intel counts execution units.
gpu.na.intel.clocks: It has no SoC clock or performance profile, and it lives inside the processor: it does not hang off a PCIe link.
gpu.na.intel.clocks.link: It has no SoC clock or performance profile.
gpu.na.intel.sensors: An Intel integrated GPU does not report its voltage, and has no separate SoC.
gpu.na.intel.throttle: This Intel generation does not publish whether the graphics engine is throttling or why; newer ones do.
gpu.na.intel.vbios: An Intel integrated GPU has no video BIOS of its own: it comes inside the machine's firmware.
gpu.na.laptop.fan: In a laptop the fan is the machine's and its controller runs it: NVIDIA does not publish it.
gpu.na.noapi: Neither Vulkan nor OpenGL uses this card on this machine, and {campos} comes from them.
gpu.na.noapi.notasked: Vulkan and OpenGL haven't been asked yet, and {campos} comes from them: they're asked when the card asleep wakes up, since asking now would wake it.
gpu.na.noapi.shared: the system memory it can take
gpu.na.notemp: This graphics card has no temperature sensor of its own.
gpu.na.novram: An integrated GPU has no memory of its own: it uses the system's, so there is no type, bus, bandwidth, data rate or Resizable BAR to report.
gpu.na.novram.clocks: With no video memory of its own there is no memory clock to show.
gpu.na.novram.sensors: With no memory chips of its own there is no memory temperature or voltage.
gpu.na.nvidia.card: NVML does not count rasterizer units or shader engines: NVIDIA's count is CUDA cores.
gpu.na.nvidia.clocks: An NVIDIA has no SoC clock or performance profile, and NVML does not give the memory's effective clock.
gpu.na.nvidia.memory: NVIDIA's driver does not publish the memory type, its bandwidth, how much the processor sees or who made the chips.
gpu.na.nvidia.sensors: On a GeForce, NVML does not publish the hotspot, the memory temperature, the regulators or the voltages; video usage is in «Right now».
gpu.na.silent.card: Neither its driver ({driver}) nor the PCI device database gives {campos} for this card.
gpu.na.virtual.card: This is a graphics device emulated by the hypervisor: it has no codename or processing units to count.
gpu.na.virtual.clocks: It has no clocks or PCIe link: there is no silicon below.
gpu.na.virtual.memory: It has no video memory of its own.
gpu.na.virtual.sensors: Nor temperatures, voltages, fan or power.
gpu.now.gap: This GPU does not report how busy {motores} is.
gpu.power.raised: It's above the factory one: someone raised it.
gpu.temp.detail: i915 and xe register hwmon only on dedicated cards, and there is no package sensor.
gpu.temp.detail.package: i915 and xe register hwmon only on dedicated cards; the temperature is the package sensor's (coretemp).
gpu.temp.none.note: This graphics card is inside the processor and has no temperature sensor of its own.
gpu.temp.package.note: This graphics card is inside the processor and has no temperature sensor of its own: the package's, which it shares with the CPU, is shown.
gpu.tip.bandwidth: How much data fits through the bus in a second: the memory rate times the bus width. It limits a card before raw compute power does.
gpu.tip.busy: How much video memory is moving right now, not how much is occupied.
gpu.tip.compute: Each vendor counts them its own way and they are not equivalent: one AMD compute unit groups dozens of the cores NVIDIA counts one by one.
gpu.tip.datarate: The real speed the data travels at. It is not the clock: GDDR6 at 1258 MHz moves sixteen transfers per cycle, that is 20 Gbps.
gpu.tip.efficient: The frequency that gets the most work per watt (RP1). Below it, power barely drops and performance does; above it, each megahertz costs more.
gpu.tip.fan.zerorpm: Many cards stop their fan while cool (zero-RPM mode) and start it as they warm up: stopped is not a fault.
gpu.tip.hotspot: The hottest point on the die, always above the edge temperature. It is what drives the fan.
gpu.tip.isa: The name of its shaders' instruction set, the one Mesa and ROCm compile for on this card.
gpu.tip.limits: Someone changed the graphics engine's minimum or maximum from what the silicon allows, by hand or with a tool. It shows here because it is the one in effect.
gpu.tip.mall: AMD's cache between the L2 and video memory: it keeps what repeats most so as not to go to VRAM.
gpu.tip.memeff: The clock the data travels at, which is the one spec sheets advertise. Memory moves several transfers per cycle of its command clock.
gpu.tip.powercap: The first is the limit in force; the other, the factory one. It can be set within that range.
gpu.tip.rebar: With Resizable BAR the CPU sees the whole card memory at once. Without it, it only reaches a 256 MiB window that the driver has to keep moving, which costs performance. It is enabled in the BIOS, and both the board and the card have to support it.
gpu.tip.rops: The ROPs, which write the finished pixels into the final image.
gpu.tip.shared: GTT: system RAM the driver lends the card when VRAM runs short. It is not graphics memory, which is why it goes separately.
gpu.tip.silmax: The highest frequency the manufacturer allows for this graphics engine (RP0). It is the stock one: above it is overclocking.
gpu.tip.silmin.efficient: On this card it is also the efficient one (RP1). {eficiente}
gpu.tip.state: Whether the firmware is cutting performance back, and why. It explains a game running worse than it should while the card looks far from its limits.
gpu.tip.videouse: The video encode and decode engines, which work separately from the rest of the GPU.
gpu.tip.visible: How much VRAM the CPU can address at once.
gpu.tip.vr: The regulators that power the chip. The system does not publish them: the card's own microcontroller counts them.
gpu.tip.vram.kept: The driver can use {total}. The card carries {chips} GiB of memory, which the box writes «{chips} GB»: the rest, {kept}, the card's firmware keeps for itself.
gpu.tip.vram.kept.driver: The driver can use {total}. The card carries {chips} GiB of memory, which the box writes «{chips} GB»: the rest, {kept}, the card and its driver reserve.
guard.cpu.fix: The interface works again with the last series built for plain x86-64:
guard.cpu.meanwhile: In the meantime this works without Qt, and dumps all the hardware to the terminal:
guard.cpu.missing: This processor is missing instructions the installed Qt needs: {banderas}
guard.cpu.override:
If you think this is wrong (some distributions build their Qt for plain
x86-64) {variable}=1 skips this check.
guard.cpu.why:
Qt {mayor}.{menor} and later require them, which leaves out Intel chips older than 2008
and AMD chips older than 2011. Nothing is wrong with your machine.
gui.description: Opens the Silux window. Without options, that is all it does.
gui.epilog.report:
The report says what the window shows, without the computer name,
addresses or serial numbers. To report a bug, attach it at
https://github.com/rcv11x/silux/issues
gui.epilog.title: In the terminal, without a window:
gui.opt.anonymous: hide what identifies the computer: name, addresses and serial numbers
gui.opt.fontscale: font size, this time only: normal, large, larger or largest
gui.opt.interval: how many seconds between readings, this time only
gui.opt.page: the page to open, by its name: CPU, Memoria, Sensores…
gui.opt.samples: how many samples before the screenshot (with --interval 1, 65 are one minute of charts)
gui.opt.screenshot: save a screenshot of the window as PNG and exit; works without a display
gui.opt.welcome: with --screenshot: the welcome over the window, on its screen N (1 or 2)
kernel.belowminimum: Your kernel ({tuyo}) is older than Linux {minimo}, the minimum Silux supports: some values may be missing without saying why.
kernel.belowminimum.title: Kernel older than {minimo}
kernel.tooold: Your kernel ({tuyo}) does not publish this; it exists since Linux {desde}.
kernel.tooold.what: {dato}: your kernel ({tuyo}) does not publish it; it exists since Linux {desde}.
lock.tip: Click the padlock to grant permissions and read it.
lock.tip.outdated: Click the padlock to update the helper: it asks for the password.
mem.channel.same: All {n} modules sit on the same channel. Split across two, the memory would move twice as much per second.
mem.channel.single: There is only one module, so memory runs at half its bandwidth. A matching second module in the other channel doubles it; on a machine with integrated graphics that shows up in the frame rate more than almost anything else.
mem.chipset: On this machine the memory is controlled by the motherboard chipset, not the processor: the board decides how fast it can go.
mem.cpumax: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s, the official maximum of the {modelo}; the modules would take {rated}. There is no profile to enable: faster is outside what the processor guarantees.
mem.maker.code: JEDEC code {codigo}, with no name in the list
mem.mixed: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s and cannot go past {lento}, which is what the slowest module gives. Another one claiming {rapido} changes nothing: they all share one clock, so the set settles at the slowest.
mem.mixed.rated: The modules are rated at different speeds ({lento} and {rapido} MT/s): all run on one clock, so the set runs at {lento} at most, the slowest's rating.
mem.title: {util} usable
mem.underclocked: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s of the {rated} it claims to support. That is usually the fast profile (XMP or EXPO) left off in the BIOS, though it can also be the processor's official limit.
mem.underclocked.chipset: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s of the {rated} it claims to support. That is usually the fast profile (XMP) left off in the BIOS, though it can also be the motherboard chipset's limit.
memory.bw.capped: Careful: this way of measuring tops out at {techo} on this machine, so your memory may be faster than that figure says.
memory.bw.hugecache: This processor's cache is so large that getting past it would ask for more memory than a program like this should reserve.
memory.bw.intro: Measures how much memory actually moves, reading a block larger than the cache. Takes a tenth of a second.
memory.bw.nocache: This processor's cache is too small to measure on its own: below a megabyte what gets timed is the call, not the memory.
memory.bw.nomem: Not enough free memory to measure without pushing something to swap.
memory.bw.note: MT/s tell you what the module is rated for, and the theoretical figure is a multiplication. This is what the machine actually achieves when reading: none reach their theoretical figure, and below half there is usually an unpopulated channel.
memory.detail.virtual: A virtual machine's memory: there are no modules to read
memory.elev.alreadyroot: The program already runs as administrator but the SMBIOS table could not be read.
memory.elev.helper: The helper that gets launched only knows how to read that table and a few processor registers: it runs no commands and writes nothing.
memory.elev.nopkexec: pkexec is not installed, so there is no way to ask for permissions.
memory.elev.nopkexec.hint: It comes with the distribution's polkit package. Running the whole program as root works too.
memory.elev.smbios: Module detail lives in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator because the machine serial numbers sit alongside those fields.
memory.elev.spd.many: The {n} modules above come from their own SPD chip, which reads without permissions. Which slot each is in, how many are free and the speed the BIOS set them to are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel keeps for the administrator.
memory.elev.spd.one: The module above comes from its own SPD chip, which reads without permissions. Which slot it is in, how many are free and the speed the BIOS set it to are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel keeps for the administrator.
memory.lat.noexec: This system does not allow executing memory reserved on the fly, which is how latency is measured.
memory.lat.note: How long an access takes when the processor cannot get ahead of it. It is what you feel when jumping around scattered data structures, and buying more memory does not improve it: it depends on the silicon and the timings.
memory.lat.nox86: Latencies are measured with a fragment of machine code that only exists for x86-64.
memory.lat.partial: RAM could not be measured: this processor's cache is so large that the chain of accesses needed does not fit in a reasonable time.
memory.lat.title: Latency by level
memory.na.ddr2.chips: A DDR2 module's SPD has no field for the chips' maker.
memory.na.nospd: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, which could not be read.
memory.na.nospd.kernel: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip. {kernel} (It is the spd5118 driver, which reads DDR5 SPD.)
memory.na.nospd.many: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, and those of modules {n} could not be read.
memory.na.nospd.one: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, and module {n}'s could not be read.
memory.na.nospd.why: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, which cannot be read: {motivo}
memory.na.nospd.why.many: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, and those of modules {n} cannot be read: {motivo}
memory.na.nospd.why.one: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, and module {n}'s cannot be read: {motivo}
memory.na.soldered: {campos} come from each module's SPD chip, and memory soldered on the board has none.
memory.na.spd.partial: {campos} are on the SPD chip's pages this machine doesn't let be read: moving past the first one takes a write to the chip, and the machine blocks it.
memory.na.voltage.profile: They run above the fastest JEDEC speed for {tipo} ({jedec} MT/s), so they use a maker's profile (XMP or EXPO): their real voltage may differ from what the BIOS says.
memory.spd.needsroot: · the slot and what they run at, with permissions
memory.spd.needsroot.one: · the slot and what it runs at, with permissions
memory.spd.notall: · the rest could not be read; it is known with permissions
memory.spd.note: The SPD is a chip every module carries with its own specifications. It says what speed it can run at, while the BIOS decides the one it actually runs at: without XMP enabled it stays on JEDEC's conservative values.
memory.spd.note.noxmp: The SPD is a chip each module carries with its characteristics. These modules carry no fast profiles: the highest speed they declare is the JEDEC one, and the BIOS decides which one they actually run at.
memory.spd.note.partial: The SPD is a chip on each module with its characteristics. Only the JEDEC profile shows here: the fast profiles, if any, are on the chip's pages this machine doesn't let be read.
memory.spd.note.short: What each module declares in its SPD chip; the BIOS decides what it really runs at.
memory.spd.note.xmpunread: The SPD is a chip each module carries with its characteristics. These modules carry an XMP profile, but this version cannot read its figures safely, so they are not shown rather than shown wrong.
memory.spd.read.many: {n} modules read from their SPD chips
memory.spd.read.one: {n} module read from its SPD chip
memory.tip.chips: Who made the silicon, which is often not who sells the module. The SPD says it, not the SMBIOS table.
memory.tip.cpumax: It runs at {actual} MT/s of the module's {rated} because {actual} is the official maximum of the {modelo}, according to the manufacturer's page.
memory.tip.ddr3l: DDR3L: the module declares in its SPD chip that it can run at 1.35 V, besides or instead of DDR3's 1.5 V.
memory.tip.elevate:
Launches a minimal helper through polkit that only knows how to read the SMBIOS table and a few processor registers.
It runs no commands and writes nothing.
memory.tip.firmware: The BIOS writes it as {mts} MT/s; same grade, rounded the other way. That is the number dmidecode shows.
memory.tip.mismatch: This module's SPD chip couldn't be read, and this is what the BIOS table says. It doesn't match what the other module's chip says: a board doesn't mix generations or form factors, and all its modules run on one clock.
memory.tip.module: SPD chip at {address} on the i2c bus. Without the SMBIOS table there is no telling which board slot it sits in, so these are numbered in reading order.
memory.tip.profiles: Timings the manufacturer guarantees above the JEDEC ones. They are detected, but their formats are not public and their figures are not decoded: guessing them would be making them up.
memory.tip.rated: What the module claims it can do, according to its own SPD chip.
memory.tip.rated.bios: What the BIOS declares in its table. The module's SPD chip, which actually knows, could not be read.
memory.tip.running: Running at {actual} MT/s of the {rated} it supports. It may be an XMP profile left off, or the processor's official memory limit, which on many models sits below what the modules can take.
memory.tip.size: Worked out from the module's own SPD chip.
memory.tip.soldered.form: The BIOS declares it as part of the board itself.
memory.tip.soldered.nospd: And it has no SPD chip, while the module in the slot does.
memory.tip.soldered.place: Its place in the BIOS's table is no slot, although the BIOS says «{formato}».
memory.tip.voltage.bios: It is the voltage the BIOS declares in its table. Many leave it at the stock value even when an XMP or EXPO profile raises the real one.
memory.tip.voltage.either: The module declares it can run at either. The board decides which, and that's in the firmware's table, read with permissions.
memory.tip.voltage.spd: The nominal voltage the module's SPD chip declares, the JEDEC one: what it is made for, not what it runs at. What it runs at comes from the firmware's table, read with permissions, if the BIOS writes it.
memory.traffic.cpu.tip: The share requested by the cores. The rest is moved by the integrated graphics and by devices, and the counter does not tell those two apart reliably.
memory.traffic.note: What the memory controller is moving right now, with the machine doing its own thing. Below is the opposite question: how much this memory can deliver when asked for everything.
module.load.always: To load it at every boot:
module.load.until_boot: “Load now” loads it until the computer shuts down, with the administrator password.
net.na.device: The kernel publishes no {fields} for this interface.
net.na.virtual: It has no {fields}: it's a virtual interface, with no card behind it.
net.none.body: No interface has a route to the network.
net.packets.misfit.why: Its packets aren't shown: its driver ({driver}) counts {media} per packet, and with an MTU of {mtu} a packet holds {maximo} bytes. It counts aggregated frames, or miscounts.
net.packets.misfit.why.nodriver: Its packets aren't shown: they count {media} per packet, and with an MTU of {mtu} a packet holds {maximo} bytes.
net.tip.dropped: Dropped are the packets the kernel itself discards when receiving or sending them: those of a protocol nothing listens to, those it filters, or those that didn't fit its queue. They are rarely losses on the wire; real ones are those that arrive with errors.
net.units.note: 1 MB/s is 8 Mb/s: speed tests use bits.
note.database: This version doesn't know it yet
note.hardware: This machine does not expose it
note.platform: Does not apply to this platform
pcie.errors.tip: What the PCIe link itself counted since boot (AER). Corrected ones are fixed by the hardware by resending; many of them point to a slot, a riser or a cable with a poor signal. Non-fatal and fatal ones are real failures.
pcie.now: Running at {actual}; the card and the slot can do {max}. At idle this is normal: the link drops to save power and rises under load.
pcie.now.lanes: Now at {actual}, at full speed but with fewer lanes than the card and the slot allow ({max}). Some cards cut them at idle; if it stays like this with the card working, the link was trained with fewer lanes: the card not fully seated, or the slot set that way in the BIOS.
perm.dialog.title: Permanent permissions
perm.explain.always: Installed, the password window will say in your language what is read and this notice won't show; the password is still asked.
perm.explain.granted: Permissions are already granted while Silux stays open.
perm.explain.once: This time: the helper works while Silux is open.
perm.explain.polkit: The password is asked by your system, not by Silux. Silux does not see it or keep it.
perm.explain.reads: Some data can only be read by the administrator: the memory modules, disk health, voltage, power and graphics usage. A small Silux helper reads it for you. It only reads; it changes nothing.
perm.explain.title: What happens when you grant permissions
perm.explain.window: This time, the system window will say that python3 is about to run as administrator: that is the Silux helper.
perm.installed: Helper installed: the password window will say in your language what is read.
perm.nopython.install: there is no system Python to install with
perm.notice.later.tip: Hides this notice until the next time you open Silux.
perm.notice.never.tip: Removes this notice for good. The link in the bar below stays.
perm.notice.title.many: {n} readings this computer does have are missing
perm.notice.title.one: {n} reading this computer does have is missing
perm.outdated.body: The installed helper is from an earlier version: update it to read this again.
perm.outdated.home: The installed helper is from an earlier version. Update it to read this data again
perm.outdated.title: The helper is out of date
perm.permanent.tip:
Installs the helper system-wide with its own polkit rule: the password window will say in your language what is read, and this notice won't show.
The password is still asked every time you grant permissions, and once to install it.
perm.polkit.message: Silux needs permission to read hardware data reserved to the administrator: memory, disks, voltage, power and graphics usage. It only reads; it changes nothing.
plat.virt.present: the processor has it ({tipo}); not in use
power.discarded: {n} impossible power readings were dropped ({fuente}). The last one: {ultima}
power.discarded.last: {vatios} W, with a ceiling of {techo} W, from subtracting {antes} from {ahora} in {segundos} s.
prov.apis.asleep: OpenGL, Vulkan and OpenCL are queried once the sleeping card wakes up.
prov.apis.asleep.hint: To list the cards they open all of them, and opening the sleeping one wakes it up.
prov.apis.asleep.title: Graphics libraries not asked yet
prov.apis.none: There is no OpenGL, Vulkan or OpenCL library to ask.
prov.apis.none.hint: Usually a machine with no graphical environment installed. The driver brings them: mesa, vulkan-radeon, vulkan-intel or the NVIDIA package.
prov.bat.nosysfs: The kernel does not publish power supply state.
prov.bat.nosysfs.hint: Without it there is nowhere to read the battery and the charger from.
prov.cppc.nobase: This machine does not publish its base clock by any route.
prov.cppc.nobase.hint: CPUID leaf 0x16 is Intel Skylake onwards, ACPI CPPC needs the firmware to declare it, and this processor's brand string carries no frequency.
prov.cppc.nobase.zen: The processor states its base clock itself, and reading it needs permissions.
prov.cppc.nobase.zen.hint: It is its P-state 0, in an MSR only the administrator reads. Neither CPUID nor ACPI CPPC publish it on this machine.
prov.cppc.nobclk: This machine does not publish its reference clock (BCLK).
prov.cppc.nobclk.hint: Only CPUID 0x16 on modern Intel or the processor's MSRs give it. Deriving it from the base clock is only reliable on ACPI CPPC platforms, where it is 100 MHz.
prov.cppc.noceiling: The top frequency of this processor is not known
prov.cppc.noceiling.hint: The firmware gives each core its place in the ranking rather than the maximum of the part, and no frequency comes out of that. With the amd-pstate driver the kernel publishes it already worked out.
prov.cppc.noceiling.source: This processor doesn't publish its factory maximum frequency.
prov.cppc.noceiling.source.hint: CPUID 0x16, on Intel since the sixth generation, and ACPI CPPC give it; this one has neither. The maximum the kernel applies is there, in its row.
prov.cpu.nocpufreq: This processor has no frequency driver (cpufreq).
prov.cpu.nocpufreq.hint: It happens when the firmware gives the system no frequency states —on some boards, with Cool'n'Quiet or SpeedStep disabled in the BIOS— or when its driver did not load; from here the two cannot be told apart. Without one, the system does not change the processor's frequency.
prov.cpu.nofreq: The kernel does not publish this processor's frequency.
prov.cpu.nofreq.vm: The hypervisor does not expose the processor frequency.
prov.cpu.nofreq.vm.hint: The host governs the clock: there is no cpufreq to read inside a virtual machine.
prov.cpu.nosysfs: The system does not publish the processor's topology.
prov.cpu.nosysfs.hint: Only happens on systems that are not Linux.
prov.cpuid.failed: The instruction that identifies the processor could not be used.
prov.cpuid.failed.hint: The system does not allow running it; what the kernel reports is used instead.
prov.cpuid.nodb: No identification database has been generated.
prov.cpuid.nosocket: The package of “{nombre}” is not in this version's table of Silux.
prov.cpuid.notech: The process node of “{nombre}” is not in this version's table of Silux.
prov.cpuid.notx86: CPUID is an x86 instruction; this machine is not x86.
prov.cpuid.notx86.hint: On ARM the identity comes from the kernel.
prov.cpuid.pin: The processor could not be read from CPU {cpu}: the system doesn't allow using it (it is offline, or a system limit prevents it).
prov.cpuid.sendreport: If you send the report (in Settings, or with --report), it goes into the next version.
prov.cpuid.unknown: This processor ({marca}) is not in this version's table of Silux, which is where its codename, process node and package come from.
prov.cpuid.unknown.hint: Everything else comes from the processor itself and is complete. If you send the report (in Settings, or with --report), it goes into the next version.
prov.crashed.hint: This is a Silux bug, not your machine's. It deserves a report.
prov.denied: The system does not let this user read this data.
prov.disk.health: Drive diagnostics are kept by each drive in its own counters.
prov.disk.health.hint: With permissions you see power-on hours, terabytes written and the wear on each one.
prov.dmi.noboard: The BIOS does not publish the board model.
prov.dmi.noboard.hint: Some manufacturers leave the field blank on purpose.
prov.dmi.none: This machine exposes no DMI information.
prov.dmi.none.hint: Happens on simple virtual machines and on many ARM boards.
prov.drm.arcusage: This card's usage is not read yet: the permissions helper only opens the integrated graphics' counter.
prov.drm.arcusage.hint: Reading an Arc's needs a change to the helper, proposed separately. Better no figure than the other card's usage.
prov.drm.asleep: The driver powers the card down while nothing uses it. On a laptop with two graphics chips (Optimus, on NVIDIA) the integrated one draws the screen, and this one powers up when a program asks for it.
prov.drm.asleep.hint: Nothing is asked of it so as not to wake it: reading it would use battery. Its memory, clocks and what its driver knows show up when something uses it.
prov.drm.asleep.title: Asleep
prov.drm.inteldriver: The system does not give this graphics card's engine usage.
prov.drm.inteldriver.detail: The {pmu} PMU publishes no busy events (*-busy).
prov.drm.inteldriver.hint: The clocks, the monitors and what Vulkan and OpenGL declare do show.
prov.drm.intelroot: The graphics card's usage and power can only be read with administrator permissions.
prov.drm.intelroot.hint: With permissions, each engine's usage and, on integrated cards, the power appear. The clocks, the monitors and what Vulkan and OpenGL declare show without asking for anything.
prov.drm.intelunopened: This graphics card's engine usage could not be read, even with permissions.
prov.drm.intelunopened.detail: The {pmu} PMU publishes *-busy events and the helper opened none.
prov.drm.intelunopened.hint: The system publishes it, but it could not be opened and from here it is not known why. The clocks, the monitors and what Vulkan and OpenGL declare do show.
prov.drm.metricsnew: This card reports telemetry in version {version}, which this program does not read yet.
prov.drm.metricsnew.hint: Throttling reasons, voltages and regulator temperatures come from there. The layout moved between versions and reading it with the previous positions would give believable, wrong numbers, so they are left out. The version is in the report: with a dump from a machine like this one it can be added.
prov.drm.nodriver: The kernel has no driver for {tarjeta}: it is falling back to the basic framebuffer.
prov.drm.nodriver.hint: The card is identified through the PCI bus, but with no driver there are no clocks, no temperature, no power draw and no memory. This happens when booting with nomodeset, with the driver not installed, or with a card newer than the kernel.
prov.drm.nodrm: {tarjeta} is held by {driver}, which does not offer it as graphics to this system.
prov.drm.nodrm.hint: It happens when it is reserved for a virtual machine (vfio-pci), or with NVIDIA's driver without nvidia-drm: its data are not read from here.
prov.drm.nogpu: No graphics card is registered with the kernel.
prov.drm.nogpu.hint: Happens on servers with no video output and in virtual machines with no emulated graphics.
prov.drm.nosysfs: The system does not show the graphics cards.
prov.drm.nosysfs.hint: It happens on systems without the kernel's graphics support.
prov.drm.nouveau: nouveau does not give the card's clocks, power or usage.
prov.drm.nouveau.hint: It is the free driver: what a program like this shows of an NVIDIA (clocks, watts, CUDA cores, throttling) comes from NVML, which ships with the proprietary driver. With nouveau you are left with the temperature, the PCIe link and the memory Vulkan reports.
prov.drm.nvidia: NVIDIA's proprietary driver does not give the card's data to the system.
prov.drm.nvidia.hint: They are read through NVML, the library the driver itself ships.
prov.drm.unbound: No driver is loaded for {tarjeta}: it is on the PCI bus, but nothing talks to it.
prov.drm.unbound.hint: Without a driver there are no clocks, temperature, power or memory. It happens with the driver not installed, with the kernel's disabled, or with a card newer than the kernel.
prov.hint.drivetemp: the temperature of the SATA drives
prov.hint.spd: the SPD of the {n} modules: XMP profiles, timings and what speed they could run at
prov.hint.spd.caution: It only reads the module's identification chip; it changes no configuration.
prov.hint.spd.one: the module's SPD: XMP profiles, timings and what speed it could run at
prov.hint.superio: fans, board voltages and chipset temperatures
prov.hint.superio.caution: Do not guess the module: every board carries a different chip and loading the wrong one can read garbage. sensors-detect identifies it and says which to load.
prov.hwmon.nochips.hint: On Intel the coretemp module enables it; on AMD, k10temp.
prov.hwmon.nocpu: No sensor chip seems to belong to the CPU.
prov.hwmon.novolt: No sensor on this machine publishes the core voltage.
prov.hwmon.novolt.hint: It usually needs the board's Super I/O module (nct6775, nct6683, it87…) or reading the VID through MSR, which requires root.
prov.imc.denied: The memory controller's traffic counter exists but cannot be read.
prov.imc.denied.hint: Uncore counters need permissions. The helper opens them without changing any system setting.
prov.imc.none: This machine does not publish memory controller traffic.
prov.imc.none.hint: Only Intel processors publish it. On AMD the kernel gives those counters no names, and a figure guessed blindly would be worse than none.
prov.imc.truncated: This machine has more memory channels than can be read at once.
prov.imc.truncated.hint: The sum would come out short, so it is not shown. This is a Silux limit: please report it with a report file.
prov.imc.unopened: The memory controller publishes its traffic, but its counter could not be opened.
prov.imc.unopened.hint: The reason goes in the report: sending it helps fix it.
prov.mem.denied: Reading the memory modules was not authorised.
prov.mem.denied.hint: You can try again whenever you like.
prov.mem.smbios: The memory modules are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator.
prov.mem.smbios.hint: With permissions you see manufacturer, part number, type, speed, ranks, voltage and which slot each module is in.
prov.mem.smbiosfail: Could not read the SMBIOS table: {error}
prov.missing: This machine does not publish this data.
prov.msr.nomodule: The «msr» module is missing, and core voltage needs it.
prov.msr.novalue: The processor gave no believable voltage in its register, so none is shown.
prov.msr.novolt: Core voltage lives in the processor, not in a board sensor.
prov.msr.novolt.hint: It is read from a processor register, and the kernel reserves that for the administrator.
prov.msr.nox86: Core voltage is read from a register that only exists on x86.
prov.msr.nox86.hint: On this architecture either the board sensor publishes it or nobody does.
prov.msr.oldintel: This processor does not publish its core voltage.
prov.msr.oldintel.hint: Intel puts it in the register that is read from the second-generation Core (Sandy Bridge) on; an earlier one does not have it, with permissions or without.
prov.nvml.nopower: The NVIDIA driver does not give this card's power draw.
prov.procfs.nostat: The system does not publish the processor's usage.
prov.rapl.denied: The RAPL energy counter exists but cannot be read.
prov.rapl.denied.hint: Many distributions have restricted it to root since CVE-2020-8694.
prov.rapl.frozen: The processor energy counter is not moving
prov.rapl.frozen.hint: Power is worked out from two readings of that counter, and it did not change between the last two. With the processor running that cannot be zero, so a 0 W reading that would not be true is not shown.
prov.rapl.none: This CPU exposes no RAPL energy counters.
prov.rapl.none.hint: It came with Intel's 2011 chips (Sandy Bridge) and AMD's Zen: older ones, ARM and virtual machines don't have it.
prov.rapl.onecore: Core power is not shown on this processor
prov.rapl.onecore.hint: On AMD that counter belongs to a single core, the first one, not to all of them added up. The package reading does cover the whole processor.
prov.smbios.nosocket: The firmware's table doesn't say either.
prov.smbios.socket.hint: With permissions it is read from the firmware's table (SMBIOS), which usually says.
prov.spd.partial: Only the first page of the memory's SPD chip can be read: reaching the others takes a write to the chip, and the machine blocks it.
prov.spd.partial.hint: That page gives the type, the speed and the JEDEC timings; the rest (maker, chips, date and profiles) can't be read on this machine.
prov.spd.readfailed: The memory's SPD chip is there, but reading it failed.
prov.spd.readfailed.hint: On DDR5 this happens when the machine blocks writes to the SPD, which the driver needs to switch pages, or when the driver did not recover after a suspend. The exact error is in the report.
prov.spd.unregistered: One module's SPD chip isn't registered: with two slots the kernel only looks for it at addresses 0x50 and 0x51, and many laptops put the second one's at 0x52.
prov.spd.unregistered.hint:
It can be registered by hand, until the next boot:
{orden}
prov.spd.unregistered.title: The kernel didn't look for a module's chip
prov.spd.unsupported: The SPD of {tipos} cannot be decoded yet.
prov.spd.unsupported.hint: The DDR4 and DDR5 formats are implemented.
prov.sys.nomeminfo: The system does not publish the memory's usage.
report.annex.intro: What Silux read from this computer without permissions, with the same things hidden as above. It lets Silux's tests reproduce the computer: there is no need to read it.
report.annex.onsave: They go at the end of the file when it is saved
report.annex.refused: {que} was still uncovered ({campos}): so as not to publish it, the raw data are left out.
report.annex.removed: Without {n} files that held something that could not be covered without breaking it: {lista}.
report.annex.removed.one: Without one file that held something that could not be covered without breaking it: {lista}.
report.annex.status.none: Without the raw data: why, at the end of the report
report.annex.title: Appendix: the raw data
report.diag.modules: Kernel modules that would show more:
report.diag.nothing: Nothing missing: everything the machine exposes was read.
report.diag.title: Diagnosis
report.head.from.source: source code or a system package
report.head.title: Silux report
report.need.database: this version doesn't know it yet
report.preview.intro: This is what gets saved: everything the window shows, page by page, without the machine's name, addresses or serial numbers. Check it before you send it.
report.preview.missing: {n} readings only the administrator can read are missing: the most useful ones to recognise your machine.
report.preview.title: The machine report
sensors.absent.gputemp: {nombre}: has no temperature sensor of its own.
sensors.alarm.crit: ⚠  It has reached the critical threshold. That is where the machine starts protecting itself.
sensors.alarm.high: ⚠  Above the high threshold. Not a fault, but worth knowing.
sensors.col.name: Sensor
sensors.driver.body.superio: With the driver of the board's Super I/O chip you would have {da}.
sensors.driver.title: A kernel driver is missing
sensors.header.tip:
Click a column to sort by it; click again to go back to
the order by device.
Drag the dividers to adjust the width.
Right-click to go back to automatic widths.
sensors.mirror: {espejo} repeats the {n} temperatures of {chip}: it is the same chip read through another driver. They are shown once, as {chip}.
sensors.placeholder: {chip}: a steady {valor} is not a measurement. It is the number the firmware returns for a thermal zone it never wired to a sensor.
sensors.tip.record:
Writes one row per sample with every sensor.
It opens in any spreadsheet, and it is how you find out
what minute something happened when you were not watching.
sensors.tip.reset:
Starts counting the extremes again from this moment.
Useful right before launching a load test.
sensors.tip.search:
Filters by sensor or device name.
“memory”, “9070”, “fan”…
sensors.title: SENSORS
sensors.unnamed.temps: {chips}: the driver numbers the temperatures without saying where each probe is. It depends on how the board maker built it, and naming them by guesswork would be making it up.
sensors.unnamed.voltages: {chips}: the driver does not say what each numbered voltage measures. It depends on how the board maker wired it, and naming them by guesswork would be making it up.
settings.allflags.help: By default only the relevant flags are shown. When enabled, all the flags CPUID returns on this machine appear; the CPU page says how many there are.
settings.allflags.label: Show every instruction set
settings.db.counts: Processor table: {intel} Intel, {amd} AMD and {arm} ARM parts from libcpuid {commit} ({fecha}); {familias} Intel families from Linux {kernel}; {modelos} AMD models from amd.com; {nodos} nodes from cpuid {cpuid}; {sockets} packages from CPU-X {cpux}.
settings.db.none: No database has been generated, so the codename and the package cannot be identified.
settings.density.help: Spacious leaves more room between rows and columns; compact tightens things up to fit more on the same screen.
settings.density.label: Density
settings.desktop.outdated.help: The entry or the icons are from another version of Silux.
settings.desktop.unsupported.help: This AppImage does not say where its file is, so there is nothing to point the entry at.
settings.fluid.help: Charts and bars glide from one reading to the next instead of jumping. Figures are not animated: they jump to the reading. It redraws more often, and costs a few percent of one core. Press space to freeze everything.
settings.fluid.label: Smooth motion
settings.fontsize.help: Scales up every bit of text. Cards and columns grow with it so nothing gets clipped.
settings.fontsize.label: Text size
settings.interval.help: Every reading walks all the machine's sensors and counters. Below half a second the cost starts to show; above two, the charts lose detail.
settings.interval.label: Refresh every
settings.language.help: Spanish is the original: when a phrase has not been translated yet, it shows in Spanish rather than blank.
settings.language.label: Language
settings.netunit.label: Network speed
settings.perm.connected.help: The helper is reading what the kernel reserves for the administrator. It goes away when Silux closes.
settings.perm.installed.connected.help: It reads what the kernel reserves for the administrator while Silux stays open. Next time you open Silux, they are granted again with the password.
settings.perm.installed.help: Permissions are granted with the password when you press the button, and the window says in your language what is read.
settings.perm.none.help: Some data, like the memory modules or the disk diagnostics, can only be read with administrator permissions.
settings.perm.notneeded.help: On this machine there is nothing that can only be read with permissions.
settings.perm.outdated.help: The helper installed in the system is not the one from this version of Silux, and it is not used. It stays owned by root until it is replaced.
settings.perm.remove.ask: The Silux helper and its polkit rule will be deleted. Afterwards, granting permissions shows the notice again and the password window shows the python3 command. Asks for the password.
settings.perm.remove.tip: Deletes the installed helper and its polkit rule. Asks for the password.
settings.perm.remove.title: Remove the helper
settings.perm.root.help: Silux is running as administrator: it reads everything without asking.
settings.perm.unsupported.help: pkexec, which asks for the password, is missing: without it there is no way to read what the kernel reserves for the administrator.
settings.share.image.help: A summary to paste in a chat or forum, without the machine name or serial numbers.
settings.share.report.help: Everything the window shows, without the machine's name or serial numbers: what you attach to a bug report, or send so Silux recognises your machine. You see it before saving it.
settings.shortcut.broken: The menu entry opens a file that no longer exists.
settings.shortcut.copied: It could not be moved, so Silux was copied to {nuevo}. The one in {viejo} can be deleted now.
settings.shortcut.desktop.help: A shortcut in the desktop folder.
settings.shortcut.dev: Development version: {ruta}, with its own entry, «Silux (development)».
settings.shortcut.elsewhere: The menu entry opens another copy of Silux.
settings.shortcut.fragile: If you move or delete this file, the shortcuts will stop working.
settings.shortcut.menu.help: Silux in the launcher, with its icon. It goes in your home folder: no permissions needed.
settings.shortcut.move.detail: It is now in {ruta}: if that file is moved or deleted, the shortcut stops working. Afterwards, Silux opens again from ~/AppImages.
settings.shortcut.move.text: So that the shortcut does not break, Silux will be moved to ~/AppImages.
settings.shortcut.move.title: Move Silux to ~/AppImages
settings.shortcut.reopen.failed: Silux is now in {ruta}, but it could not be opened from there: {error}
settings.tempunit.label: Temperature unit
settings.theme.label: Theme
settings.tip.report:
Generates a text file with all the detected hardware and, above all, with what could not be read and why. It is what to attach when reporting a bug.

It leaves out the machine name, the IP and MAC addresses and the serial numbers.
settings.updates.channel.help: With «Testing», test versions (like 0.4-prueba2) are offered too; with «Stable», only finals. A test version gets its final on either.
settings.updates.help: Off by default: Silux connects to nothing unless you ask. When on, it asks GitHub (api.github.com, the rcv11x/silux repository) for the latest version at startup, without sending anything about this computer. It never updates until you press «Update».
settings.updates.label: Check for updates at startup
settings.updates.manual: Check whether there is a new version
settings.welcome.help: The screen shown on first launch.
settings.welcome.label: Welcome
share.failed: The image could not be saved
share.footer: Made with Silux · no identifying data included
share.tip:
An image summarising this machine, ready to paste into a chat or a forum.
It carries no hostname, addresses or serial numbers.
spd.nobus: The SMBus controller exists but the kernel has not enabled it: the board firmware keeps that bus to itself.
spd.nobus.hint: The kernel enables it with acpi_enforce_resources=lax in its boot parameters, but there is a risk: the firmware and the kernel end up using the same chip without coordinating, and on some boards that gives false sensor readings or hangs. It is not worth it just to see this reading.
spd.nochip: The memory's bus is there, but the kernel has registered no SPD chip on it.
spd.nochip.hint: With no chip registered there is no driver to load: loading ee1004 or spd5118 would change nothing.
spd.nocontent: The SPD chips have their driver, but the kernel doesn't publish what they hold.
spd.nocontent.hint: Why can't be told from here: it may be the kernel's version or how its driver was built.
spd.nodriver: The memory's SPD chip is there, but no driver reads it.
spd.nodriver.hint:
Depending on the memory the machine carries:
  sudo modprobe spd5118    (DDR5)
  sudo modprobe ee1004     (DDR4)
  sudo modprobe at24       (DDR3 and earlier)
spd.nodriver.load: It is read by loading its driver:  {orden}
spd.nosmbus: This board exposes no SMBus controller, which is the bus the modules' SPD chips are read over.
spd.nosmbus.hint: Happens on laptops and on boards where the firmware keeps it to itself. There is no way to read it from the system.
status.blocked.outdated: Helper out of date · update it
status.blocked.tip:
The kernel keeps some data for the administrator: memory module details, disk health and processor power draw.
They are requested once and read without changing anything.
storage.bar.reserved.tip: What the filesystem keeps for itself: in ext4, the 5 % it reserves for root (so the system can still write with the disk full) and its own tables. It is neither used nor free for anyone else.
storage.bar.swap.tip: A partition the system uses as swap memory: it isn't mounted like the rest, but it's in use.
storage.health.body: Power-on hours, terabytes written and wear are kept by each drive in its own diagnostic counters. The kernel reserves those commands for the administrator because they are the same ones used to erase a drive.
storage.health.hint: The helper that gets launched only knows how to ask for diagnostics and read a few system tables: it runs no commands and writes nothing.
storage.health.read: Diagnostics read from {n} of {total} drives. The rest do not publish them or did not answer.
storage.na.flash: A USB flash drive reports no temperature or diagnosis.
storage.na.hdd.life: A spinning disk has no “life left”: that is the wear of an SSD's cells.
storage.na.kind.usb: Over USB it isn't known whether a disk spins or is an SSD: the kernel marks nearly everything on that bus as spinning.
storage.na.vendor: The disk doesn't say its maker, neither in its model nor in what the kernel publishes.
storage.na.virtual: This is a virtual disk: it has no temperature, hours, total written or wear of its own, and what it would answer to a diagnosis is made up by the hypervisor.
storage.na.written: This disk does not count what has been written in its SMART.
storage.na.written.unit: The totals written and read are not shown: this disk's counter says less than what it already holds, so it counts in a unit that is not known.
storage.subtitle: {tam} used across {n} mounted partitions
storage.tip.kind: No field states it: it is worked out from whether the kernel considers the drive rotational and which bus it hangs off.
storage.tip.life: What the drive itself reckons it has left, according to its own wear counter.
storage.tip.nolimits: This disk declares no temperature limits, so its figure has no colour: Silux doesn't make them up.
storage.tip.notemp: A SATA disk only gives its temperature two ways: its diagnostics (SMART), which need permissions, or the kernel's drivetemp module (sudo modprobe drivetemp).
storage.tip.notemp.nvme: This disk does not publish its temperature.
storage.tip.physical: Modern drives work in 4 KiB sectors internally even while telling the system they are 512 B.
storage.tip.scheduler: How the kernel orders requests before sending them to the drive. On an NVMe it is usually off because the drive itself does it better.
storage.tip.templimits: The disk's own (on an NVMe, its warning and critical temperatures; on a SATA disk, its SCT ones through drivetemp). From the warning the temperature shows in amber, and from the critical one in red.
storage.tip.trim: Whether the drive accepts discards and what can be seen of them being issued. The timer may be enabled and still not cover this drive.
storage.tip.written: The TBW: how much data has been written to this drive since it left the factory. It is what consumes an SSD's life.
storage.title: {tam} across {n} drives
storage.warn.hint: The drive itself says so in its diagnostic log. Worth having a copy of whatever is inside.
sys.boot.nofirmware: How long the firmware and the loader take is missing: {gestor} does not publish it, and neither does the firmware.
sys.boot.nofirmware.unknown: How long the firmware and the loader take is missing: neither the boot loader nor the firmware publishes it.
sys.boot.nosystemd: How long the kernel and userspace take is missing: systemd provides it, and it did not answer.
sys.boot.notsystemd: How long the kernel and userspace take is missing: systemd measures that, and this system boots with {init}.
sys.boot.unfinished: Userspace has not finished booting yet.
sys.boot.unpublished: This machine's boot loader does not publish its name or its timings (systemd-boot, Limine and some distributions' GRUB do).
sys.kernel.name: Kernel
sys.na.desktop.both: Neither the desktop nor the graphical session is known: the environment Silux was opened from doesn't declare them.
sys.na.desktop.one: {what} isn't known: the environment Silux was opened from doesn't declare it.
sys.subtitle: {equipo} · up {tiempo}
sys.swap.label: Swap
sys.taint.0: a module under a license not compatible with the GPL
sys.taint.11: a workaround for a firmware bug
sys.taint.7: the kernel died recently (OOPS or BUG)
sys.taint.tip: The kernel marks itself tainted when something happens that means its bugs will only be looked at by whoever caused it. Its value: {mask}.
sys.tip.apps: Total minus free, buffers and reclaimable cache. It comes out slightly below «Used» because that one includes what cannot be given back.
sys.tip.cache: Reclaimable disk cache: Cached + SReclaimable − Shmem.
sys.tip.used: Total minus available. Free alone is not subtracted because on Linux the kernel uses every spare byte as cache, and gives it back the moment something asks for it.
sys.vuln.list: The ones that affect this processor, as the kernel describes them
temp.limits.declared: Limits the sensor declares: {limites}. Below the warning the figure has no colour; from the warning, amber, and from the critical one, red.
throttle.unknown: a reason it does not report
updates.done: Silux {version} is in place and verified. Restart now?
updates.done.title: Updated
updates.err.badhash: the download does not match its SHA-256 sum, and was deleted
updates.err.badreply: GitHub sent a reply that cannot be read
updates.err.insecure: a redirect tried to leave HTTPS
updates.err.network: there is no connection to GitHub or it dropped
updates.err.noasset: the new version has no AppImage of this kind
updates.err.nocerts: the system's certificates to check GitHub against are not there: they come in the package ca-certificates
updates.err.nosums: the new version does not publish its SHA256SUMS
updates.err.notls: this copy lacks what secure connections need (TLS)
updates.err.toolarge: the file is over the size limit
updates.err.write: the AppImage folder could not be written
updates.manual: This copy cannot replace itself ({motivo}). Download it from {url}
